capture-anchored-pacing: Thread C laid its capture ticks on an even grid unrelated to when the display presented, so at a pace equal to the refresh a picture waited up to a period for the next tick, and a display slightly faster than the pace lost a present now and then as the grid drifted. The pacer now takes a dated picture as it arrives, within a quarter period early and creeping at most 1/64 of a period, keeping the 3/4-period floor and the 64/63 long-run bound; undated pictures keep the old grid exactly. Windows dates pictures by DXGI's LastPresentTime and shows a still desktop's first frame; Mac dates them by their arrival from ScreenCaptureKit. The Backend and VideoSource traits gain the seams later changes use (submitted_picture, capture_poll, video_paused, retune), with defaults that keep embedders working, and a desktop_capture_pacing debug event reports the wait.
win-keep-awake: A view-only viewer's picture froze when the Windows host's display-off timeout fired, a Modern Standby laptop could sleep under a session, and a remote pointer move did not wake a dark display. While a session captures, the host now holds display-required and system-required power requests, turns a dark display on when capture starts or resumes, and releases both about 2 s after capture stops. Each capture call and pointer read only stores a time; a parked watchdog thread does the rest.
helper-pipe-transfer: Each record crossing the helper's two named pipes went out as four writes, the service relayed it in 8 KiB copies, and mio 1.2.4 read named pipes in small chunks, so a keyframe took many completions per hop. A record is now one vectored write, the relay uses 256 KiB buffers toward the app, the pipes get 256 KiB quotas, and mio 1.2.5 reads in large chunks. The bytes on the pipe and HELPER_PROTOCOL are unchanged; pipe_relay_bench measures the path on a Windows device.
win-sendinput-moves: SetCursorPos is not input: low-level hooks and raw-input readers saw nothing, the idle timer never advanced, a dark display did not wake, and a remote drawing got one point per message pump. Windows hosts now inject pointer moves as absolute SendInput over the virtual desktop. The 250 ms settle logic the Mac host used moves to shared code, so both report the injected pixel until a read shows it.
rate-model-latch: The timestamp rate model latched only after two 3 s windows at a low pace, so an encoder that budgets per second overspent for 6 s or more after every pace drop, and a bits-per-frame cut inside a window could latch a per-frame encoder by mistake. The latch now integrates sent against expected bits over the last 2 s of 250 ms ticks, compares each tick at the higher of its two bits-per-frame values, and latches a per-second encoder within about 2 s while never latching a per-frame one. The slow-link suite gains per-second-encoder cases that assert both.
viewer-fps-cap: A viewer slower than its host overshot every few seconds, and an age backlog dropped the queue and froze the picture until the next keyframe. The fps cap now measures what the decoder takes over its last busy ticks and remembers that capacity, raises in steps scaled to the ceiling (so a 120 FPS session recovers from a transient backlog in seconds), and drains a moderate age backlog instead of discarding it, keeping the IDR reset for a deep one. No protocol, FFI or runner change, and no allocation per unit.
direct-cooldown: The pause after a direct fallback lived in each consumer, and every connect_tcp built a new one, so each viewer session or reconnect behind a symmetric NAT or blocked UDP paid the punch setup again. A Client and its carrier siblings now keep the direct pause and the LAN-TCP pause per service, so a fallback sends the client's later connections to that service straight to the relay until the pause ends, a direct success clears it, or the network changes.
relay-tcp-tuning: Linux restarts a TCP connection's congestion window after idle, so the first burst after a still period on a relayed session slow-starts again, and Cubic on a lossy relay-to-viewer leg can fall below every preset's rate. The Docker image and an opt-in install step turn net.ipv4.tcp_slow_start_after_idle off, the relay notes at startup when it is on, and a new --tcp-congestion option (PB_MAPPER_TCP_CONGESTION) sets a congestion control such as bbr on the relay's listener. Both are off by default.
viewer-decoder-stats: The Mac viewer reported no decode time, CPU or hardware flag and the Linux viewer no timings, so the native presenters and GPU conversion could not be checked in the field. The Mac viewer now reports decode time, decoder CPU, whether the decoder is hardware, and its window's refresh; the Linux viewer reports surface-consume time and the refresh rate; and the quality panel shows decode or convert time on every desktop viewer. Clocks are read only while the panel asks for timings.
linux-gpu-convert: The Linux viewer downloaded every hardware-decoded picture to system memory, converted it to RGBA on the CPU and uploaded the RGBA to Flutter. Pictures now stay NV12 or I420 and are converted once in Flutter's GL context through an FlTextureGL; with GStreamer 1.24 or later, dma-buf pictures are imported as EGLImages and never touch the CPU. Only a converted picture earns its presentation receipt, a context that cannot convert ends the session as decoder_failed, and the runner module's ABI goes to 2. CI installs Mesa's EGL and GL ES so the harness checks the conversion on llvmpipe, which caught that a snapshot's RGBA needs the picture's frame rate for GStreamer's converter.
native-cursor: A controlling viewer over a custom pointer shape hid the OS pointer and had Flutter paint the bitmap, which trailed the hand by Flutter's frame pipeline, and a shape change waited for a rebuild. The Windows, macOS and Linux viewers now turn the host's bitmap into a native cursor through a pb_mapper/desktop_pointer channel and switch shapes without waiting for a frame, keeping painting only as a fallback; cursors are cached per device pixel ratio and padded so the hotspot lands exactly on Linux.
viewer-pixel-snap: Original size and a fitted 1:1 picture could sit at fractional offsets, so bilinear sampling blurred one-pixel text strokes, which alternated between sharp and blurred as the pointer moved. Every desktop viewer now keeps a 1:1 picture on the device-pixel grid and shows a fit within 4% of 1:1 at exactly 1:1, as airhand does.
